      "research_question": "How do knowledge workers manage person-to-person requests across organizational contexts and communication channels, and what implications do those practices have for request-management system design?",

      "paper_id": "doi-10-18653-v1-2026-acl-long-1149",
      "title": "Agent Newsroom: Efficient Chronological Report Generation via Dynamic Multi-Agent Collaboration",
      "research_question": "Can chronological report generation be organized as dynamically scheduled, budget-aware multi-agent collaboration that improves semantic coverage, temporal grounding, and narrative balance while reducing inference cost?",
      "methodology": "The paper introduces MAS-TLS, a multi-agent timeline-summarization system organized around a master editor and specialized reporter agents in a star topology. Its collaborative cycle includes editorial assignment, time-anchored evidence-grounded investigation and drafting, cross-agent scrutiny and adjudication, and adaptive orchestration; allocation and scheduling mechanisms are designed to promote coverage and diversity while respecting token and time budgets. The system is evaluated on the Crisis, Entities, and T17 timeline-summarization benchmarks against traditional and LLM-based baselines, using AR-1, AR-2, Date-F1, token use, inference time, temporal-balance, and topical-balance measures. The authors also conduct component ablations and transfer studies across model backbones and languages.",
      "key_findings": [
        {
          "finding": "MAS-TLS improves most reported semantic-coverage and temporal-grounding measurements across the three benchmarks, although it does not dominate every individual metric; on T17 its AR-2 result is 2.8% below the strongest compared baseline.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Section 4.2, Overall Performance"
        },
        {
          "finding": "On the Entities benchmark MAS-TLS uses 13.8 million tokens and 37,078 seconds, compared with 20.2 million tokens and 39,009 seconds for the strongest efficiency-oriented baseline CHRONOS, while also obtaining higher AR-1.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Section 4.3, Efficiency Analysis"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The reported temporal and topical distribution measures indicate that MAS-TLS produces more balanced timelines, including lower inter-event temporal variation and topic distributions closer to the reference timelines.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Section 4.4, Balance Analysis"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Ablation experiments show that removing distinctiveness or the LLM-based ranking/adjudication component causes substantial quality losses, while disabling adaptive scheduling increases token consumption by about 34%.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Section 5.1, Ablation Study"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Across tested model backbones the paper reports less than 8% relative variation in AR-1, and its cross-lingual experiments retain a semantic-coverage advantage over the strongest compared baseline.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Section 5.3, Transferability"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Evidence grounding remains imperfect: the authors report unsupported-event rates of roughly 5.3% to 7.9% across the evaluated benchmarks.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Section 5.4, Evidence Support"

      "paper_id": "manual-50ed5dc808",
      "title": "The Learning Behind Gmail Priority Inbox",
      "research_question": "How can Gmail learn a scalable, continuously updated, user-specific ranking of email importance from noisy behavioral feedback and explicit corrections?",
      "methodology": "The system models email importance primarily as the probability that a user will act on a message within a defined time window, using hundreds of social, content, thread, and label-related features. It combines a global logistic model with per-user model adjustments and updates models online using a passive-aggressive learning procedure, while a separately personalized decision threshold controls which messages are presented as important. The production architecture logs message features and subsequent user actions and performs distributed model updates over Gmail infrastructure. Evaluation includes implicit-feedback accuracy, approximately 160,000 explicit user importance markings, and a time-use comparison involving about 2,000 Google employees with similar email volume.",
      "key_findings": [
        {
          "finding": "Email importance is strongly personalized, motivating a model that combines globally learned patterns with per-user parameter adjustments and per-user thresholds.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Introduction; Learning Models; Ranking and Thresholds"
        },
        {
          "finding": "On approximately 160,000 explicit user importance markings, the reported error rate falls from 45% for a global model to 38% with user-specific models and to 31% when personalized thresholds are also used.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Evaluation"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Implicit-feedback evaluation yields accuracy of about 80% with roughly five percentage points of variation, while the authors identify presentation bias of about two to three percentage points among active Priority Inbox users.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Evaluation"
        },
        {
          "finding": "False-negative importance errors occur approximately three to four times as often as false positives under the implicit-label evaluation, illustrating asymmetric behavior and the importance of threshold selection.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Evaluation"
        },
        {
          "finding": "In a comparison of roughly 2,000 Google employees with similar mail volume, Priority Inbox users spent about 6% less time reading email overall and about 13% less time reading messages classified as unimportant.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Evaluation"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Manual importance corrections are used as higher-confidence feedback and can adjust an individual user's importance threshold in real time.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Learning Models; Ranking and Thresholds"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The batch-oriented production implementation is reported to process model updates at approximately 35 users per second per core, avoiding the cost of keeping a continuously active learner for every user.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Production System"
        }
      ],
      "limitations": [
        "Implicit interaction labels are noisy because opening or replying to a message is not identical to judging it important.",
        "Presentation of Priority Inbox itself affects user behavior, creating measurable presentation bias in implicit evaluation.",
        "Explicit user corrections are informative but are biased toward cases where the system previously made an error.",
        "The employee time-use comparison is not presented as a randomized controlled experiment, so the observed time differences do not by themselves establish causation.",
        "Actions occurring after the configured maximum observation window do not become positive training examples.",
        "The target is personalized importance or action likelihood rather than an explicit distinction between obligation, preference, commitment, and discretionary interest.",
        "The paper relies on proprietary Gmail interaction data and does not provide a public evaluation dataset."

        "code_available": false,

        "The system treats importance as user-specific rather than assigning the same priority to a message for every recipient.",
        "Training labels are derived largely from actions users take after messages arrive.",
        "The learner uses hundreds of message, social, thread, content, and label features.",
        "A global model supplies transferable information while each user's model learns deviations from that global behavior.",
        "Online passive-aggressive updates allow models to adapt as new behavioral evidence arrives.",
        "Users differ in the relative cost they place on false positives and false negatives.",
        "Personalized thresholds substantially reduce disagreement with users' explicit importance markings.",
        "Implicit feedback is useful but contains presentation and interpretation biases.",
        "Priority Inbox users in the reported employee comparison spent less time on email, especially on messages considered unimportant.",
        "The production design batches model updating to make millions of personalized models operationally feasible."
      ],
      "source_url": "https://static.googleusercontent.com/media/research.google.com/en//pubs/archive/36955.pdf",
      "access": "full_text"
    },
    {
      "paper_id": "doi-10-1016-j-knosys-2013-02-015",
      "title": "Exploiting relevance, coverage, and novelty for query-focused multi-document summarization",
      "research_question": "Can query-focused multi-document summaries be improved by jointly modeling dependent relevance, content coverage, novelty, and topic balance rather than treating sentence relevance independently?",
      "methodology": "The paper proposes PRCN, an unsupervised extractive framework built from PLSA and PHITS that uses a query-aware reference topic model to estimate dependent sentence relevance and topic coverage. Relevance and coverage are represented probabilistically, while additional document-side and query-side relevance and novelty features are constructed explicitly; model parameters are estimated with expectation maximization. A greedy sentence-selection procedure imposes topic and query balance while constructing the final summary. The approach is evaluated on the DUC 2005 and DUC 2006 query-focused multi-document summarization benchmarks using ROUGE measures.",
      "key_findings": [
        {
          "finding": "The paper argues that sentence utility is dependent on what has already been selected or seen, and PRCN therefore replaces the usual independent-relevance assumption with probabilistic dependent relevance.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Section 1, Introduction; Section 3, Problem Definition and Solution"
        },
        {
          "finding": "PRCN jointly represents relevance, topic coverage, and novelty rather than optimizing query relevance alone.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Sections 3-5"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The sentence-selection stage uses a greedy balancing procedure intended to preserve suitable proportions of document and query topics while limiting redundancy.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Section 5, Feature Construction and Topic Balance Imposition"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Experiments on DUC 2005 and DUC 2006 report that PRCN outperforms the compared methods on ROUGE-2 and ROUGE-W by a statistically described significant margin.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Section 6, Experimental Evaluation"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The approach is unsupervised and extractive, so its coverage and novelty decisions are made by selecting source sentences rather than generating new text.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Section 2, Query-Focused Multi-Document Summarization"
        }
      ],
      "limitations": [
        "Evaluation is restricted to the DUC 2005 and DUC 2006 query-focused summarization benchmarks, so generalization beyond those news-oriented datasets is not established by the reported experiments.",
        "The method operates on a static document collection and does not model temporal state transitions or supersession of previously summarized work items.",
        "The method is extractive and therefore does not address factual support problems introduced by free-form generation.",
        "ROUGE-2 and ROUGE-W measure lexical overlap and do not directly evaluate evidence completeness, lifecycle-state correctness, or joint omission and repetition.",
        "The approach depends on latent-topic and bag-of-words-style preprocessing assumptions, including stopword removal and stemming.",
        "No publicly released implementation is identified in the article."
      ],
      "reproducibility": {
        "code_available": false,
        "dataset_available": true,
        "metrics_reported": true
      },
      "confidence_scores": {
        "dependent_relevance": 0.98,
        "joint_relevance_coverage_novelty": 0.99,
        "topic_balance": 0.98,
        "duc_improvement": 0.96,
        "extractive_unsupervised": 0.99
      },
      "raw_claims": [
        "A useful query-focused summary must balance relevance to the query with coverage of the source documents.",
        "Selecting one sentence can change the utility of selecting another sentence later.",
        "PRCN models relevance and coverage within a common probabilistic framework.",
        "The query is incorporated into a reference topic model used to estimate dependent relevance.",
        "Novelty features are used to discourage redundant information.",
        "The model includes features defined from both document and query perspectives.",
        "A greedy selection algorithm is used to maintain topic balance while choosing summary sentences.",
        "Model estimation uses an expectation-maximization procedure.",
        "The evaluation uses the DUC 2005 and DUC 2006 query-focused summarization datasets.",
        "The reported experiments favor PRCN over the compared methods on ROUGE-2 and ROUGE-W."
      ],
      "source_url": "https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0950705113000804",
      "access": "full_text"
    },
    {
      "paper_id": "manual-0839b98ee7",
      "title": "Can requests-for-action and commitments-to-act be reliably identified in email messages?",
      "research_question": "Can human annotators reliably and repeatably identify both the presence and strength of requests-for-action and commitments-to-act in workplace email, making these categories plausible targets for automated detection?",
      "methodology": "The authors conduct an exploratory annotation study on 54 email messages containing 310 sentences drawn from the Enron email corpus and selected to expose varied explicit and implicit request and commitment phenomena. Three coders annotate every sentence in its message context for the presence and strength of Requests-for-Action and Commitments-to-Act, while also considering a designated recipient and classifying messages by audience type. The email is preprocessed to remove signatures and quoted or forwarded text and is sentence-segmented before annotation, with annotators able to flag preprocessing errors. Agreement is measured with pairwise and three-way kappa statistics, followed by qualitative error analysis of systematic disagreements.",
      "key_findings": [
        {
          "finding": "Three-way agreement for identifying whether a sentence contains a Request-for-Action is relatively high at kappa 0.78.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Section 5, Results and Discussion"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Agreement on Request-for-Action strength is lower but still tentative at kappa 0.60.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Section 5, Results and Discussion"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Commitments-to-Act are substantially harder to annotate consistently: presence agreement is kappa 0.54 and strength agreement is kappa 0.37.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Section 5, Results and Discussion"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Agreement varies with audience structure; single-recipient messages generally produce the highest agreement, while closed-group messages produce the lowest, with Commitment-to-Act agreement particularly weak for closed groups.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Section 5, Results and Discussion"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Conditional offers are a major systematic ambiguity and account for almost 40% of disagreements about whether a Commitment-to-Act is present.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Section 6.1, Conditional Offers"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Implicit requests and missing organizational relationship context create additional ambiguity, including uncertainty about whether an utterance creates an obligation and how strong that obligation is.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Sections 6.2-6.3"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Annotator error flags suggest a sentence-segmentation error rate of at least 10% on the pilot email data, much worse than the segmenter's reported performance on a biomedical corpus.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Section 5, Results and Discussion"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The authors conclude that the task appears repeatable enough to motivate automation, but they plan to refine the categories and run a substantially larger annotation study before building classifiers.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "Section 7, Conclusions and Future Work"
        }
      ],
      "limitations": [
        "The study is explicitly a small pilot with only 54 messages and 310 sentences.",
        "The three annotators were the paper's authors rather than a broad independent annotator pool.",
        "The authors state that the small sample prevents firm conclusions about differences between audience types.",
        "Fine-grained strength labels have relatively weak agreement, especially for Commitments-to-Act.",
        "Conditional offers, implicit requests, and missing sender-recipient relationship information produce systematic ambiguity.",
        "Quoted and forwarded conversation history was removed during preprocessing even though such context can be necessary for interpreting conversational structure.",
        "Sentence segmentation performed poorly on the email data, with annotator flags indicating at least a 10% error rate.",
        "The study establishes annotation feasibility rather than the accuracy of an automatic classifier.",
        "It labels request and commitment expressions within messages but does not track whether the corresponding work item later becomes fulfilled, resolved, cancelled, or superseded."
      ],
      "reproducibility": {
        "code_available": false,
        "dataset_available": true,
        "metrics_reported": true
      },
      "confidence_scores": {
        "rfa_presence_agreement": 0.99,
        "rfa_strength_agreement": 0.99,
        "cta_agreement": 0.99,
        "audience_effect": 0.95,
        "conditional_offer_ambiguity": 0.99,
        "relationship_context": 0.97,
        "segmentation_error": 0.98,
        "automation_feasibility": 0.95
      },
      "raw_claims": [
        "A Request-for-Action is defined as language that places an expectation or obligation on a recipient to respond or act.",
        "A Commitment-to-Act is defined as language indicating that the sender takes responsibility for some future action being performed.",
        "The same sentence can contain both a request and a commitment.",
        "Annotators identify requests more consistently than commitments.",
        "Annotators agree more on whether an obligation exists than on how strong it is.",
        "Commitment strength is particularly difficult to annotate reliably.",
        "Messages addressed to several identifiable recipients create more ambiguity about who is responsible for an action.",
        "Conditional offers are a recurring source of disagreement about commitments.",
        "Implicit speech acts require interpretation of surrounding message context.",
        "Organizational hierarchy can change how annotators interpret the strength of an apparent obligation.",
        "Generic sentence segmentation tools can transfer poorly to informal workplace email.",
        "The authors regard the pilot results as encouraging but insufficient and plan broader annotation before automated classification."
      ],
      "source_url": "https://www.researchgate.net/publication/228649541_Can_requests-for-action_and_commitments-to-act_be_reliably_identified_in_email_messages",
      "access": "full_text"
    }
  ],
  "skipped": []
}
